passage:
Tanuja: you alive? haven't seen you in 3 weeks
Wasim: barely. deadlines at the firm. I eat lunch at my desk
Tanuja: that's sad
Tanuja: we're flying kites on the terrace this Sunday. like old times
Wasim: kites?? I'm 22 not 10
Tanuja: exactly why you need it
Wasim: I have a report due Monday
Tanuja: 2 hours. then go back to your report
Wasim: fine. 2 hours
Wasim: (Sunday night) ok I haven't laughed like that in months
Wasim: my kite got cut in 5 mins and I still had fun
Tanuja: told you 😄
Wasim: also finished half the report after. my brain felt lighter
Tanuja: next month. same terrace
Wasim: deal 🪁

qa.q: How long had it been since Tanuja saw Wasim?
qa.a: 3 weeks.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel after the kite flying?
qa.a: Wasim felt lighter and happier, laughing more than in months even though the kite got cut.

qa.q: Why was Tanuja's '2 hours' offer a smart way to convince Wasim?
qa.a: It respected Wasim's deadline while still giving a real break, so saying yes felt manageable.

qa.q: What would change if Wasim kept eating lunch at the desk and skipping every weekend?
qa.a: Wasim would likely become more drained and less productive, since the fun break actually helped get half the report done.

grounding: Shows a young adult rediscovering playful fun as a counterweight to work stress, nudged by a friend.

passage: Minakshi, twenty-two, had been teaching at the small-town government school for a year, and lately she'd stopped smiling. Lesson plans, inspections, parents at the gate. One Friday evening, as she walked home past the school ground, a group of kids and a few young men were playing kabaddi in the dust. Her cousin Nilesh waved. "Didi, we're one short!" She laughed and shook her head, but he wouldn't stop calling. She tucked her dupatta, kicked off her sandals and joined in. Within minutes she was shouting "kabaddi, kabaddi" and tagging two boys before getting caught, laughing so hard she had to sit down. Walking home with dusty feet, she realised her shoulders didn't ache for the first time in weeks.

qa.q: What game were the kids and young men playing?
qa.a: Kabaddi.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's laughter and relaxed shoulders suggest about her?
qa.a: She had been carrying a lot of stress, and play let her release it and feel light again.

qa.q: How could Minakshi keep this balance going?
qa.a: She could join the Friday games regularly or find other small moments of fun between her teaching work.

qa.q: How might Nilesh see his cousin joining the game?
qa.a: He was probably delighted and surprised to see his serious teacher cousin laughing and playing.

grounding: Shows a young teacher rediscovering play as a relief from work stress in her small town.

passage: In Lagos, Chidi, twenty-two, a junior nurse on night shifts, had started to feel like a machine. Work, sleep, work. His sister Ada noticed he'd stopped telling jokes at dinner. One Saturday she dragged him to an afrobeat dance class at a community hall. "I can't dance," he protested. "Nobody here can," she said. The instructor had them copying moves that made everyone look silly. Chidi tripped over his feet, bumped into Ada, and burst out laughing for the first time in weeks. By the end, he was sweaty and grinning. On the bus home, he found himself humming the music. "Same time next week?" Ada asked. "Only if you promise to look as bad as me," he said.

qa.q: Where was the dance class held?
qa.a: At a community hall.

qa.q: What might Chidi have been feeling before the class?
qa.a: He seemed drained and flat, like a machine, from constant work and night shifts.

qa.q: What small step helped Chidi feel lighter?
qa.a: Trying a playful, low-pressure activity with his sister where no one had to be good, which let him laugh again.

qa.q: How might Ada feel seeing her brother laugh again?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and happy, since she had noticed him stop joking and wanted him back. 🙂

grounding: Shows a young adult abroad rediscovering play and humour as balance against work stress.

passage: By the third week of the product launch, the office on the ninth floor had gone silent except for keyboards. Sachin, twenty-two, had been eating lunch at his desk and dreaming about spreadsheets. On Friday his colleague Yash dragged an old carrom board out of the storeroom and set it on the pantry table. 'Fifteen minutes. One game. Loser buys chai.' Sachin said he had a report due. Yash flicked the striker toward him. Sachin sighed, sat down, and missed three easy shots in a row. Yash did a dramatic slow-motion celebration. Sachin laughed so hard he snorted, which set off the two interns watching. He lost, bought the chai, and went back to his desk. The report took him half the time he had expected.

qa.q: Where did Yash find the carrom board?
qa.a: In the storeroom.

qa.q: Why did Sachin say he had a report due?
qa.a: He felt so pressured by work that he believed he couldn't spare even fifteen minutes to play.

qa.q: What could Sachin and Yash do to keep this balance going?
qa.a: They could make the Friday game a short regular ritual, so play is part of the week rather than a rare break.

qa.q: How might the interns watching experience this moment?
qa.a: They would see their colleagues laughing, which could ease their own stress and make the office feel friendlier. 😊

grounding: Shows young adults using a short game and laughter to counter work stress during a busy launch.

passage:
Dear Mridul,
Remember the silly comic strips we used to draw in the back of our physics notebooks? The one about the angry pressure cooker? I found them while moving flats last week, and I laughed so loudly my new neighbour knocked to check on me. It made me realise I haven't done anything just for fun in about a year. It's been job, commute, sleep, repeat, and I've been snapping at everyone. So I bought a cheap sketchbook, and every night now I draw one silly panel before bed. Last night it was my boss as a sleepy owl. No one will ever see it. My shoulders have come down from my ears a bit. Shall we restart the strip? You do the words, I'll draw, like old times. 🙂
Sumit

qa.q: What did Sumit find while moving flats?
qa.a: The old comic strips from their physics notebooks.

qa.q: What did Sumit realise after laughing at the old comics?
qa.a: Sumit realised that a year of only job, commute and sleep had squeezed out fun and left a stressed, snappish feeling.

qa.q: Why is one silly panel a night a good habit for Sumit?
qa.a: It is small enough to keep up daily, and it gives Sumit regular lightness that eases the stress.

qa.q: How might Mridul feel receiving this letter?
qa.a: Probably amused and happy to be remembered, and tempted to restart the strip together.

grounding: Illustrates a young adult bringing back a playful hobby as a counterweight to work stress.
